BACKGROUND: The accuracy of multidetector computed tomographic angiography (CTA) for the diagnosis of acute pulmonary embolism has not been determined conclusively. METHODS: The Prospective Investigation of Pulmonary Embolism Diagnosis II trial was a prospective, multicenter investigation of the accuracy of multidetector CTA alone and combined with venous-phase imaging (CTA-CTV) for the diagnosis of acute pulmonary embolism. We used a composite reference test to confirm or rule out the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism. RESULTS: Among 824 patients with a reference diagnosis and a completed CT study,

CTA was inconclusive in 51 because of poor image quality. Excluding such inconclusive studies, the sensitivity of CTA was 83 percent and the specificity was 96 percent. Positive predictive values were 96 percent with a concordantly high or low probability on clinical assessment, 92 percent with an intermediate probability on clinical assessment, and nondiagnostic if clinical probability was discordant. CTA-CTV was inconclusive in 87 of 824 patients because the image quality of either CTA or CTV was poor. The sensitivity of CTA-CTV for pulmonary embolism was 90 percent, and specificity was 95 percent. CTA-CTV was also nondiagnostic with a discordant clinical probability.

CONCLUSIONS: In patients with suspected pulmonary embolism, multidetector CTA-CTV has a higher diagnostic sensitivity than does CTA alone, with similar specificity. The predictive value of either CTA or CTA-CTV is high with a concordant clinical assessment, but additional testing is necessary when the clinical probability is inconsistent with the imaging results. BACKGROUND: A fixed-dose regimen of rivaroxaban, an oral factor Xa inhibitor, has been shown to be as effective as standard anticoagulant therapy for the treatment of deep-vein thrombosis, without the need for laboratory monitoring. This approach may also simplify the treatment of pulmonary embolism.

METHODS: In a randomized, open-label, event-driven, noninferiority trial involving 4832 patients who had acute symptomatic pulmonary embolism with or without deep-vein thrombosis, we compared rivaroxaban (15 mg twice daily for 3 weeks, followed by 20 mg once daily) with standard therapy with enoxaparin followed by an adjusted-dose vitamin K antagonist for 3, 6, or 12 months. The primary efficacy outcome was symptomatic recurrent venous thromboembolism. The principal safety outcome was major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding. RESULTS: Rivaroxaban was noninferior to standard therapy (noninferiority margin,

2.0; P=0.003) for the primary efficacy outcome, with 50 events in the rivaroxaban group (2.1%) versus 44 events in the standard-therapy group (1.8%) (hazard ratio, 1.12; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.75 to 1.68). The principal safety outcome occurred in 10.3% of patients in the rivaroxaban group and 11.4% of those in the standard-therapy group (hazard ratio, 0.90; 95% CI, 0.76 to 1.07; P=0.23). Major bleeding was observed in 26 patients (1.1%) in the rivaroxaban group and 52 patients (2.2%) in the standard-therapy group (hazard ratio, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.31 to 0.79; P=0.003). Rates of other adverse events were similar in the two groups.

CONCLUSIONS: A fixed-dose regimen of rivaroxaban alone was noninferior to standard therapy for the initial and long-term treatment of pulmonary embolism and had a potentially improved benefit-risk profile. BACKGROUND: Apixaban, an oral factor Xa inhibitor administered in fixed doses, may simplify the treatment of venous thromboembolism.

METHODS: In this randomized, double-blind study, we compared apixaban (at a dose of 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, followed by 5 mg twice daily for 6 months) with conventional therapy (subcutaneous enoxaparin, followed by warfarin) in 5395 patients with acute venous thromboembolism. The primary efficacy outcome was recurrent symptomatic venous thromboembolism or death related to venous thromboembolism. The principal safety outcomes were major bleeding alone and major bleeding plus clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding.

RESULTS: The primary efficacy outcome occurred in 59 of 2609 patients (2.3%) in the apixaban group, as compared with 71 of 2635 (2.7%) in the conventional-therapy group (relative risk, 0.84; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.60 to 1.18; difference in risk [apixaban minus conventional therapy], -0.4 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.3 to 0.4). Apixaban was noninferior to conventional therapy (P<0.001) for predefined upper limits of the 95% confidence intervals for both relative risk (<1.80) and difference in risk (<3.5 percentage points). Major bleeding occurred in 0.6% of patients who received apixaban and in 1.8% of those who received conventional therapy (relative risk, 0.31; 95% CI,

0.17 to 0.55; P<0.001 for superiority). The composite outcome of major bleeding and clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding occurred in 4.3% of the patients in the apixaban group, as compared with 9.7% of those in the conventional-therapy group (relative risk, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.36 to 0.55; P<0.001). Rates of other adverse events were similar in the two groups. CONCLUSIONS: A fixed-dose regimen of apixaban alone was noninferior to conventional therapy for the treatment of acute venous thromboembolism and was associated with significantly less bleeding (Funded by Pfizer and Bristol-Myers Squibb; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00643201). Pleuritic chest pain is characterized by sudden and intense sharp, stabbing, or burning pain in the chest when inhaling and exhaling. Pulmonary embolism is the most common serious cause, found in 5% to 21% of patients who present to an emergency department with pleuritic chest pain. A validated clinical decision rule for pulmonary embolism should be employed to guide the use of additional tests such as d-dimer assays, ventilation-perfusion scans, or computed tomography angiography. Myocardial infarction, pericarditis, aortic dissection, pneumonia, and pneumothorax are other serious causes that should be ruled out using history and physical examination, electrocardiography, troponin assays, and chest radiography before another diagnosis is made. Validated clinical decision rules are available to help exclude coronary artery disease. Viruses are common causative agents of pleuritic chest pain. Coxsackieviruses, respiratory syncytial virus, influenza, parainfluenza, mumps, adenovirus, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus are likely pathogens. Treatment is guided by the underlying diagnosis. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are appropriate for pain management in those with virally triggered or nonspecific pleuritic chest pain. In patients with persistent symptoms, persons who smoke, and those older than 50 years with pneumonia, it is important to document radiographic resolution with repeat chest radiography six weeks after initial treatment.

Venous thromboembolism, comprising both deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, is a chronic illness that affects nearly 10 million people every year worldwide. Strong provoking risk factors for venous thromboembolism include major surgery and active cancer, but most events are unprovoked. Diagnosis requires a sequential work-up that combines assessment of clinical pretest probability for venous thromboembolism using a clinical score (eg, Wells score),

D-dimer testing, and imaging. Venous thromboembolism can be considered excluded in patients with both a non-high clinical pretest probability and normal D-dimer concentrations. When required, ultrasonography should be done for a suspected deep vein thrombosis and CT or ventilation-perfusion scintigraphy for a suspected pulmonary embolism. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are the first-line treatment for almost all patients with venous thromboembolism (including those with cancer). After completing 3-6 months of initial treatment, anticoagulation can be discontinued in patients with venous thromboembolism provoked by a major transient risk factor. Patients whose long-term risk of recurrent venous thromboembolism outweighs the long-term risk of major bleeding, such as those with active cancer or men with unprovoked venous thromboembolism, should receive indefinite anticoagulant treatment. Pharmacological venous thromboembolism prophylaxis is generally warranted in patients undergoing major orthopaedic or cancer surgery. Ongoing research is focused on improving diagnostic strategies for suspected deep vein thrombosis, comparing different

DOACs, developing safer anticoagulants, and further individualising approaches for the prevention and management of venous thromboembolism. Copyright © 2021 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved. We have previously demonstrated that a clinical model can be safely used in a management strategy in patients with suspected pulmonary embolism (PE). We sought to simplify the clinical model and determine a scoring system, that when combined with D-dimer results, would safely exclude PE without the need for other tests, in a large proportion of patients. We used a randomly selected sample of 80% of the patients that participated in a prospective cohort study of patients with suspected PE to perform a logistic regression analysis on 40 clinical variables to create a simple clinical prediction rule. Cut points on the new rule were determined to create two scoring systems. In the first scoring system patients were classified as having low, moderate and high probability of

PE with the proportions being similar to those determined in our original study. The second system was designed to create two categories, PE likely and unlikely. The goal in the latter was that PE unlikely patients with a negative D-dimer result would have PE in less than 2% of cases. The proportion of patients with

PE in each category was determined overall and according to a positive or negative SimpliRED D-dimer result. After these determinations we applied the models to the remaining 20% of patients as a validation of the results. The following seven variables and assigned scores (in brackets) were included in the clinical prediction rule: Clinical symptoms of DVT (3.0), no alternative diagnosis (3.0), heart rate >100 (1.5), immobilization or surgery in the previous four weeks (1.5), previous DVT/PE (1.5), hemoptysis (1.0) and malignancy (1.0). Patients were considered low probability if the score was

4.0. 7.8% of patients with scores of less than or equal to 4 had PE but if the D-dimer was negative in these patients the rate of PE was only 2.2% (95% CI = 1.0% to 4.0%) in the derivation set and 1.7% in the validation set. Importantly this combination occurred in 46% of our study patients. A score of <2.0 and a negative D-dimer results in a PE rate of 1.5% (95% CI = 0.4% to 3.7%) in the derivation set and 2.7% (95% CI = 0.3% to 9.0%) in the validation set and only occurred in 29% of patients. The combination of a score < or =4.0 by our simple clinical prediction rule and a negative SimpliRED D-Dimer result may safely exclude PE in a large proportion of patients with suspected PE.

Background In patients with acute pulmonary embolism (PE), hypoxia may increase pulmonary vascular resistance and worsen right ventricular dysfunction (RVD), which is a key prognostic factor. However, associations between hypoxia, RVD and clinical outcomes have not been well described.
Aim To describe associations between hypoxia, RVD and clinical outcomes in patients with PE.

Methods We performed a retrospective, single-center cohort study of patients treated by the Massachusetts General Hospital Pulmonary Embolism Response Team (PERT) from 10/2012 to 08/2021. Inclusion criteria included confirmed PE, recorded oxygen saturation prior to PERT activation, and echocardiogram within three days of PERT activation. Patients were categorized into four subgroups based on (1) hypoxia status (SaO₂ below vs. above 95%) and, (2) oxygen support (below vs. above 3 L/min). Our primary outcome was the presence of RVD on echocardiogram. Our secondary outcome was clinical deterioration within 7 days.

Results We included 894 PE patients. The mean age was 61 (± 16 SD), 614/894 (69%) were hypoxic, and 624/894 (70%) had RVD on echocardiogram. Overall, hypoxic patients were more likely to have RVD than non-hypoxic patients (467/614 [76%] vs. 157/280 [56%], p < 0.0001). On subgroup analysis, RVD prevalence was highest in the “hypoxic with oxygen support ≥3L” group ( n = 216/266, 81%) followed by the “not hypoxic with oxygen support ≥3L” group 53/70 (76%); 198/278 (71%) in the “hypoxic with oxygen support <3L” and 157/280 (56%) in the “not hypoxic with oxygen support <3L” groups. Clinical deterioration occurred in 199/894 (22%) patients and was more common in hypoxic patients than non-hypoxic patients (157/614 [26%] vs. 42/280 [15%], p < 0.0001), and most common in the “hypoxic with oxygen support ≥3L” subgroup 88/266 (33%).

Conclusions Hypoxia is associated with RVD and clinical deterioration in patients with PE. More research is needed to understand the risk associated with hypoxia and the physiology of supplemental oxygen support in PE. Clinical trial number Not applicable. Severe PE manifests as both hemodynamic and respiratory compromise. The combination of mechanical obstruction and pulmonary vasoconstriction, which is worsened by hypoxia, increases pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR). The resulting right ventricular (RV) pressure overload leads to increased RV workload and reduced RV coronary perfusion resulting in RV oxygen demand/supply mismatch and RV myocardial ischemia. This sequence may manifest as right ventricular dysfunction (RVD), which is directly linked to mortality and is considered the primary cause of death in severe PE. Accordingly, both hypoxia and RVD play significant roles in the vicious cycle of acute PE pathophysiology [ 1 , 4 , 5 ].

Hypoxia in patients with PE represents not only a risk factor but also a potential therapeutic target. A recent study of a porcine model of PE showed that supplemental oxygen reduced PVR and improved RV function [ 6 ]. Similar effects were observed in a clinical trial of supplemental oxygen in patients with acute PE [ 7 ]. There is a lack of studies linking hypoxia with RVD and outcomes, especially considering subgroups based on O 2 saturation and O 2 supplementation, which reflect the realities of clinical practice in which most hypoxic PE patients are treated with supplemental oxygen.

In this study, we aimed to investigate the associations between hypoxia, RVD, and clinical deterioration in patients with acute PE. We hypothesized that hypoxia or the need for supplemental oxygen would be associated with more frequent RVD and worse clinical outcomes.

Methods Study design and data acquisition We performed a retrospective, single-center cohort study. We enrolled all patients for whom the Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) pulmonary embolism response team (PERT) was activated from October 2012 to August 2021. MGH is an urban, academic tertiary care center. Since its inception in 2012, the PERT at MGH has followed a multidisciplinary approach to the treatment of PE [ 8 ]. The goal of the PERT is to quickly enlist the assistance of multiple specialists to assess a patient with PE, mobilize resources, and facilitate advanced treatment when needed [ 9 ]. PERT is activated at the treating physician’s discretion not dictated by any protocol. Data describing each patient evaluated by the MGH PERT is entered in a web-based registry (REDCap™, www.projectredcap.org ) [ 10 ]. The MGH PERT data registry captures information related to patient demographics, clinical presentation, diagnostic procedures, treatment, and outcomes across several follow-up timepoints. The registry is approved by the MassGeneralBrigham IRB (protocol number 2016P000179) under a waiver of informed consent as a retrospective database.

Inclusion and exclusion criteria We included patients with Computed Tomography Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA)-confirmed PE, a recorded oxygen saturation from pulse oximetry at the time of PERT activation, and an echocardiogram performed within three days of PERT activation. We excluded patients who underwent advanced interventions such as systemic thrombolysis, catheter-based intervention, surgical embolectomy, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) before the echocardiogram was performed as these interventions could influence the presence of RVD on echocardiogram.

Definitions of hypoxia, RVD and outcomes We defined hypoxia based on the lowest oxygen saturation (SaO 2 ) and the maximal amount of oxygen support the patient required during the 12 h prior to PERT activation. Significant oxygen supplementation was defined as: 3L or more per minute by nasal cannula, use of a nonrebreather mask, continuous or biphasic positive pressure ventilation (CPAP or BIPAP), or mechanical ventilation. Non-hypoxic patients had an SaO 2 ≧95% and oxygen supplementation below 3L per minute. In a 2 × 2 manner, we further divided the patients into four subgroups: (1) SaO 2 <95% with supplemental oxygen; (2) SaO 2 <95% without supplemental oxygen; (3) SaO 2 ≧95% with supplemental oxygen; and (4) SaO 2 ≧95% without supplemental oxygen. Patients were defined as “hypoxic” if they belonged to groups 1, 2 or 3.

The primary outcome was the presence of RVD on echocardiogram performed within the first 3 days following PERT activation. RVD was defined as RV dilatation, RV free wall hypokinesis, septal bowing, or right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) > 36 mmHg [ 11 ]. Our secondary outcome was a 7-day composite outcome of clinical deterioration defined as all-cause mortality, treatment with systemic intravenous (IV) thrombolysis, a catheter-based intervention (thrombolysis or thromboembolectomy), surgical thromboembolectomy, or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), or hypotension requiring vasopressors.

Statistical analysis Categorical variables are presented as frequencies with percentages and continuous variables with standard deviations. We compared characteristics of hypoxic and non-hypoxic patients using Fisher’s exact and T-tests for categorical and continuous variables, respectively, to identify potential confounders to include in multivariable models. We compared outcomes between patient subgroups defined by hypoxia and/or oxygen support using Fisher’s exact test and logistic regression. We performed multivariable logistic regression adjusting for age, coronary artery disease (CAD), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), family history of deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism (DVT/PE), and smoking status. Additionally, we stratified patients into subgroups based on presence vs. absence of hypoxia and RVD to assess the association between these factors and clinical deterioration. SAS version 9.4 was used for all analyses. The significance level for statistical tests was set at 0.05 without adjustment for multiple comparisons due to the exploratory nature of the analyses.

Results A total of 1551 patients were enrolled in the MGH PERT data registry, of whom 894 (58%) patients met our inclusion criteria (Fig. 1 ). The mean age was 61 (± 16) years. The median time from PERT activation to TTE was 15.6 h (IQR 2.0–46.0). Of the 657 patients we excluded from the study, 274 (42%) had no imaging-confirmed PE, 213 (32%) did not have a recorded echocardiogram within three days of PERT activation, 72 (12%) received advanced interventions prior to the echocardiogram and 90 (14%) met criteria for clinical deterioration before PERT activation. Of 894 patients included in the study, 614 (69%) were hypoxic and 199 (22%) had clinical deterioration. Patient characteristics are in Table 1 .

Primary outcome There were 624/894 (70%) patients who had RVD on echocardiogram of which 436 (70%) had RV dilatation, 392 (63%) had RV free wall hypokinesis, 295 (47%) had septal bowing, and 379 (61%) had RVSP > 36 mmHg. Table 2 shows that the prevalence of RVD was significantly higher in hypoxic patients than in non-hypoxic patients ( n = 467 [76%] vs. n = 157 [56%], p < 0.0001; unadjusted odds ratio (OR) 2.49 [95% CI 1.84–3.36]). On multivariate analysis, hypoxia remained associated with RVD, with odds of RVD 2.49 times higher in hypoxic patients compared to non-hypoxic patients (OR 2.49 [95% CI 1.83–3.41], p < 0.0001) The remaining co-variates are presented in Supplementary Table 1 with significant associations for age and COPD. Comparisons of individual subgroups of hypoxia are available in Supplementary Table 2 . Within the subgroups of hypoxia, RVD was most prevalent ( n = 216, 81%) in group 1 (SaO 2 <95% and oxygen support ≥3L). The prevalence of RVD was second highest in group 3 (SaO₂ ≥95% with oxygen support ≥3L) ( n = 53, 76%) and was followed by group 2 (SaO₂ <95% with O₂ support <3L) ( n = 198, 71%). The lowest prevalence of RVD was observed in group 4 (SaO₂ ≥95% with O₂ support <3L) ( n = 157, 56%). Hypoxia remained associated with each of the four components encompassing RVD (see Supplementary Table 3 ).

Discussion Among patients with acute PE, we found hypoxia to be independently associated with both RVD and clinical deterioration. When patients present with hypoxia, standard clinical practice requires oxygen supplementation, so it is challenging to independently assess the effect of hypoxia and supplemental oxygen use. We therefore used a definition that both combines and separates oxygen saturation and oxygen supplementation. Our findings show that hypoxia despite oxygen supplementation is most strongly associated with RVD and clinical deterioration.

Hypoxia in acute pulmonary embolism Acute PE causes ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxia due to which triggers hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction leading to an increase in RV afterload. The normal RV is very susceptible to acute pressure overload, which can result in RV dilation which increase wall tension and myocardial work and oxygen demand. However, both the increased RV pressure and wall tension and a low systemic and coronary blood pressure compromises RV myocardial perfusion and thereby oxygen supply. Hypoxemia worsens the supply. Collectively, the RV will experience a oxygen supply-demand mismatch causing RV ischemia, impaired systolic function, and ultimately RV failure which is cause of death in acute PE [ 12 , 13 ].

Oxygen supplementation may modulate this pathophysiology by counteracting some of the hemodynamic consequences of hypoxia. We have previously demonstrated that supplemental oxygen is associated with a reduced pulmonary vascular resistance and improved RV function in an animal model of acute PE [ 6 ]. If oxygen have similar effects in human PE remain unknown, but clinical data have shown promising effects as well and further studies are pending [ 7 , 14 , 15 ]. Oxygen is known to reduce pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure in human related conditions such as pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) [ 14 , 16 – 18 ]. emphasizing the potential of supplemental oxygen in human PE.

Association between hypoxia and right ventricular function and outcome In this study, we found hypoxia associated with both RVD and clinical deterioration. This confirms previous findings by Subramanian et al. who reported hypoxia to be associated with of RVD and 30-day mortality [ 5 ]. Grifoni et al. also demonstrated that PE patients with RVD were more likely to be hypoxic [ 10 ].

Hypoxia is not included in all PE risk stratification models, nor is routine oxygen supplementation recommended for patients with SaO₂ > 90% [ 1 ]. The simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (sPESI) does include hypoxia < 90% as an independent risk factor associated with 30-day mortality in patients with PE [ 19 , 23 ]. However, other scores, as the Bova score, do not include hypoxia [ 19 , 21 , 24 ] We chose a stricter 95% cut-off and still found a robust association between hypoxia and adverse outcomes, and our results highlight the potential role of hypoxia in PE risk stratification. Contrary to the potential therapeutic effects of oxygen supplementation, our study shows that patients receiving oxygen were more likely to have RVD and experience clinical deterioration. However, this likely reflects confounding by indication, as the decision to provide supplemental oxygen often signifies more symptomatic PE.

We also found an association between hypoxia and clinical deterioration. This is comparable to prior studies of both intermediate-risk [ 12 , 25 ] and high-risk[ 5 , 24 ] acute PE. Our data confirm the well described association between RVD and clinical deterioration [ 26 , 27 ]. However, the present study adds the higher risk of clinical deterioration among patients with both RVD and hypoxia suggesting a synergistic interaction of these pathophysiological factors. Our results may aid clinical decision-making, since the data suggest that PE patients presenting with hypoxia, especially if not easily corrected by supplementary oxygen, are at higher risk of developing RVD and clinical deterioration. Clinicians could consider (persistent) hypoxia as a warning sign warranting closer observation, but such strategy needs to be confirmed in a prospective study.

Limitations Our study has several limitations that warrant consideration. This study is a retrospective analysis of a prospective registry, so cannot establish causality. We also compared oxygen saturations and supplementation measured prior to PERT activation, though some echocardiographic data were not collected until after PERT activation. Furthermore, we did not have data on previous echocardiograms could therefore not distinguish between pre-existing RVD or RVD caused by the index PE. The presence and severity of hypoxia may have influenced clinicians determining the urgency of treatment and the need for advanced therapeutic interventions. Because we excluded patients who did not have echocardiograms prior to an advanced intervention, this could have introduced bias by excluding patients with low saturations from our analysis. However, that bias would most likely have driven our results towards the null, so we do not think this had a significant effect. Lastly, the study was conducted at a single center in Boston only including patients for whom PERT was activated, i.e. typically patients with central PE, high clot burden, RVD or other high-risk factors. This selection bias and limited generalizability affect any direct translation of our results to an overall PE population.

Conclusion Our study demonstrated an association between hypoxia, RVD, and clinical deterioration in patients with acute PE. This association was particularly pronounced in patients who were hypoxic despite oxygen support. These findings underscore the importance of further research into the management of hypoxia in PE patients. Pulmonary embolism (PE) is increasingly recognized as an episode of care that extends well beyond hospital discharge. Current guidance is distributed across several documents: the 2019 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines; the 2026 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) multisociety guideline, which replaced the massive/submassive terminology with clinical categories A–E; and separate position papers on catheter-directed intervention (CDI) and on follow-up. This narrative review (i) provides a side-by-side comparison of the ESC and AHA/ACC risk frameworks and their therapeutic implications; (ii) updates the evidence on reperfusion, including the recent randomized trials HI-PEITHO, PEERLESS and STORM-PE; and (iii) focuses on transitions of care and long-term follow-up, which guidelines address less comprehensively. Anticoagulation, preferably with a direct oral anticoagulant, remains the treatment for most patients. Systemic thrombolysis is reserved for high-risk (ESC) or category E (AHA/ACC) PE, because in intermediate-risk disease it halves hemodynamic decompensation at the cost of a several-fold increase in major and intracranial bleeding, without long-term functional benefit. In HI-PEITHO, ultrasound-facilitated catheter-directed thrombolysis reduced a 7-day composite outcome driven by cardiorespiratory decompensation (4.0% vs. 10.3%) in intermediate-high-risk patients with additional markers of physiological stress, without intracranial hemorrhage; a survival benefit of CDI has not been demonstrated. At discharge, a minimum bundle should specify the drug, dose, anticipated duration, provoking context, bleeding mitigation and follow-up ownership, followed by early contact within one week and a structured review at approximately three months. Up to half of survivors report persistent dyspnea or exercise limitation, whereas chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) develops in approximately 2%–3%. Persistent symptoms should prompt phenotype-directed evaluation with echocardiography, ventilation/perfusion scintigraphy, cardiopulmonary exercise testing and, when indicated, right-heart catheterization interpreted with the 2022 hemodynamic definitions, followed by early referral to an expert center where pulmonary endarterectomy, balloon pulmonary angioplasty and medical therapy can be combined. We state the type of evidence underpinning each key recommendation, propose a discharge bundle, a structured follow-up algorithm and episode-wide quality indicators, and identify the evidence gaps that should guide future trials. anticoagulation catheter-directed intervention chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension post-pulmonary embolism syndrome pulmonary embolism risk stratification thrombolysis venous thromboembolism The author(s) declared that financial support was received for this work and/or its publication. Although age-standardized PE-related mortality in the European Union approximately halved between 2000 and 2015 ( 2 ), PE remains associated with early death, recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE), treatment-related bleeding and substantial post-acute morbidity ( 1 , 3 , 4 ).

The care gap increasingly lies after initial survival. Up to half of patients report persistent dyspnea, reduced exercise capacity or impaired quality of life months after the index event ( 5 , 6 ), and in the prospective FOCUS cohort the two-year cumulative incidence of post-PE impairment was 16.0% ( 7 ). Only a minority develop chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), but distinguishing deconditioning, comorbidity, persistent right ventricular (RV) dysfunction, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease (CTEPD) and CTEPH requires a structured pathway, and fragmented follow-up delays the diagnosis of operable disease ( 4 , 8 ).

Several authoritative documents already address parts of this pathway ( Table 1 ). The 2019 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines ( 1 ) and the 2026 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) multisociety guideline ( 9 ) cover diagnosis, risk stratification and acute treatment; the 2022 ESC position paper on follow-up ( 4 ) and the European Respiratory Society (ERS) statement on CTEPH ( 8 ) cover the post-acute phase; the 2022 ESC/ERS pulmonary hypertension guidelines define the hemodynamic thresholds ( 10 ); and recent consensus documents address catheter-directed interventions ( 11 , 12 ). The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline itself spans diagnosis through follow-up, but these documents were developed in parallel and use different terminology—most visibly the ESC four-tier risk model versus the AHA/ACC clinical categories A–E—and a systematic comparison of international guidelines has identified areas of harmony, dissonance and silence, including the absence of a universal definition of shock in PE ( 13 ). The contribution of this review is therefore not to restate guideline recommendations, but to provide three elements that are not available in any single document: (i) an explicit side-by-side comparison of the European and American risk frameworks, with particular attention to the clinical implications of the new categories C–E, including incipient cardiopulmonary failure and normotensive shock; (ii) an evidence-graded update of acute reperfusion, incorporating the randomized trials of catheter-directed intervention (CDI) published since 2022 and stating the type of evidence that supports each key recommendation; and (iii) an operational framework linking acute decisions to longitudinal follow-up, consisting of a minimum discharge bundle with an acute-phase handover dataset, a phenotype-directed post-PE pathway and episode-wide quality indicators. The integrated pathway is summarized in the central illustration ( Figure 1 ).

Includes flowcharts for diagnosis, risk stratification by AHA/ACC risk categories, transition of care recommendations, structured three-month review distinguishing asymptomatic individuals from those with persistent dyspnea, and a five-step approach for managing symptoms after three months, covering screening, imaging, physiological assessment, classification, and treatment. 2 Materials and methods PubMed/MEDLINE was searched for English-language publications in adults from 1 January 2000 to 31 August 2026, complemented by the websites of major cardiovascular, hematology, emergency medicine and respiratory societies for guidelines and consensus documents, and by ClinicalTrials.gov for ongoing randomized trials. The search combined “pulmonary embolism” or “venous thromboembolism” with terms for each domain of the review (diagnosis, risk stratification, anticoagulation, thrombolysis, catheter-directed intervention, mechanical thrombectomy, embolectomy, extracorporeal support, response teams, follow-up, post-pulmonary embolism syndrome, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease and hypertension, balloon pulmonary angioplasty and rehabilitation); the full search strings are provided in Supplementary Table S1 . Because generic terms failed to retrieve some recent trials in the initial search, the search was repeated during revision and supplemented by searches for the names of individual trials and registries ( Supplementary Table S1 ), forward citation tracking of the 2026 AHA/ACC guideline and the 2022 ESC follow-up position paper, and screening of the reference lists of key publications.

Eligible sources were, in descending order of priority, clinical practice guidelines and society consensus documents, randomized controlled trials and their meta-analyses, prospective cohort and management studies, and large registries; smaller observational studies were included only when higher-level evidence was lacking. Case reports, conference abstracts and unpublished data were excluded. Because the review was intended to integrate clinical practice rather than to estimate pooled effects, appraisal was qualitative and no meta-analysis or formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed. To make the evidence hierarchy explicit, the type of evidence supporting each key recommendation is stated in the text and summarized in Section 11 , and statements for which no supporting evidence was identified are labeled as the authors' opinion.

3 Pathophysiology across the acute-to-chronic continuum 3.1 Thrombus formation and provoking context Most pulmonary emboli originate in the deep veins of the lower limbs or pelvis, reflecting a variable combination of venous stasis, endothelial perturbation and hypercoagulability ( 1 ). A major operation creates a strong exposure that disappears, whereas cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome, chronic inflammatory disease or persistent immobility continue to generate risk; acute infection and critical illness act mainly as transient provoking factors ( 14 ). Because the provoking context determines the risk of recurrence once anticoagulation stops, it should be recorded precisely rather than reduced to the labels “provoked” and “unprovoked” ( 14 , 15 ).

3.2 Right ventricular failure and normotensive shock Clinical severity is determined by the interaction between embolic obstruction and the capacity of the RV to adapt, rather than by the anatomical extent of obstruction alone ( 1 , 9 ). Acute pressure overload produces RV dilatation, increased wall stress and oxygen demand, septal displacement with reduced left ventricular filling and, through systemic hypotension, a lower right coronary perfusion gradient, initiating a self-reinforcing cycle of RV ischemia and failure ( 1 ). This explains why patients with limited reserve may decompensate after a smaller embolus, and why the AHA/ACC guideline advises against using thrombus burden for risk stratification ( 9 ). Compensatory vasoconstriction can maintain systolic pressure despite falling cardiac output, producing normotensive shock with rising lactate, oliguria or altered mentation; an elevated plasma lactate in normotensive patients is independently associated with adverse short-term outcomes ( 16 ). Hypoxemia results from ventilation/perfusion mismatch, low mixed venous oxygen saturation and, occasionally, right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale, so oxygen saturation is not a stand-alone measure of embolic severity ( 1 ).

3.3 From acute embolus to chronic thromboembolic disease In most patients, thrombus resolves substantially during the first months of anticoagulation. In a minority, organized thrombus becomes incorporated into the arterial wall as webs, bands, stenoses, pouch lesions and occlusions; flow is redistributed and a secondary small-vessel arteriopathy can develop in unobstructed territories, increasing pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) ( 8 , 17 ). The RV initially adapts through hypertrophy and later decompensates as reserve is exhausted. Because symptoms evolve gradually, chronic disease is frequently recognized late, which is the rationale for structured follow-up after acute PE ( 4 , 8 ).

4 Diagnosis 4.1 Pre-test probability and D-dimer Diagnostic testing should begin with explicit estimation of clinical probability ( 1 , 9 ). In patients with low or intermediate pre-test probability, a negative highly sensitive D-dimer safely excludes PE. An age-adjusted threshold (age × 10 µg/L above 50 years) increased the proportion of patients aged ≥75 years in whom PE could be excluded from 6.4% to 29.7%, with a three-month failure rate of 0.3% ( 18 ). The YEARS strategy, which combines three clinical items with probability-adapted D-dimer thresholds, avoided computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) in 48% of patients, compared with 34% under the conventional algorithm, with a three-month VTE rate of 0.61% among patients in whom PE was excluded without imaging ( 19 ). The pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria (PERC) are appropriate only in patients with very low clinical probability; in this population the PROPER cluster-randomized trial showed non-inferiority, with a three-month VTE rate of 0.1% ( 20 ). A pregnancy-adapted YEARS algorithm avoided CTPA in 39% of pregnant women with a three-month VTE rate of 0.21% ( 21 ). A positive D-dimer is not diagnostic and is particularly nonspecific in hospitalized patients, cancer, pregnancy, infection and advanced age; infection and critical illness also elevate troponin and natriuretic peptides, which should be considered when these biomarkers are used for risk stratification ( 1 ).

4.2 Imaging strategy CTPA is the reference imaging test for most adults because it confirms emboli, depicts RV enlargement and may identify alternative diagnoses ( 1 , 9 ). Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy remains important when iodinated contrast is contraindicated, when radiation to breast tissue is a major concern (for example, in young women and during pregnancy), and when chronic thromboembolic obstruction is suspected ( 1 , 22 ). Compression ultrasonography can establish VTE when proximal deep-vein thrombosis (DVT) is demonstrated, but a negative examination does not exclude PE. Bedside echocardiography is not a rule-out test in stable patients; in shock, however, acute RV pressure overload can justify immediate reperfusion when transport to definitive imaging is unsafe ( 1 ). The principal diagnostic tools are summarized in Table 2 . CTPA also provides early clues to pre-existing chronic disease—eccentric wall-adherent defects, webs, bands, mosaic perfusion or enlarged bronchial arteries—which should be reported because they change the follow-up plan ( 8 , 10 ).

4.3 Incidental and isolated subsegmental pulmonary embolism The AHA/ACC guideline assigns asymptomatic, incidentally detected PE to a separate category A ( 9 ). Incidental PE detected during cancer staging carries a meaningful recurrence risk and is treated like symptomatic PE when segmental or more proximal ( 23 , 24 ). Isolated subsegmental PE is more difficult, because small defects are susceptible to artifact while treatment exposes patients with a low absolute recurrence risk to bleeding. In a prospective management study of 266 patients with subsegmental PE and no proximal DVT managed without anticoagulation, the 90-day rate of recurrent VTE was 3.1%, higher than anticipated, with a higher rate among patients with multiple subsegmental defects ( 25 ). On this evidence, surveillance without anticoagulation is defensible only for a single subsegmental defect confirmed by expert review, with negative bilateral proximal ultrasonography, adequate cardiopulmonary reserve, no active cancer or other persistent risk factor, and assured follow-up; multiple defects, reduced reserve, ongoing risk factors or inability to provide surveillance favor anticoagulation ( 1 , 3 , 25 , 26 ).

5 Risk stratification: European and American frameworks 5.1 The 2019 ESC model The ESC model first identifies high-risk PE, defined by hemodynamic instability: cardiac arrest, obstructive shock [systolic blood pressure (SBP) < 90 mmHg or vasopressor requirement with end-organ hypoperfusion], or persistent hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg or a drop ≥40 mmHg for >15 min not explained by other causes) ( 1 ). Normotensive patients are then classified using the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI) ( 27 ) or its simplified version (sPESI), RV dysfunction on echocardiography or CTPA, and cardiac troponin. Intermediate-high risk requires both RV dysfunction and an elevated troponin; intermediate-low risk applies when one or neither is present in a patient with PESI class III–V or sPESI ≥1, or when either is present despite a low clinical score; low risk requires a low clinical score without RV dysfunction or troponin elevation when these are assessed ( 1 ). Quantitatively, sPESI 0 identified a 30-day mortality of 1.0% versus 10.9% for sPESI ≥1 ( 28 ), and elevated troponin was associated with a more than five-fold increase in short-term mortality (odds ratio 5.24) ( 29 ). The Hestia criteria address a different question, namely whether home treatment is feasible (Section 7.1 ) ( 30 ).

5.2 The 2026 AHA/ACC clinical categories The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline abandoned the terms massive and submassive and introduced five clinical categories with subcategories ( Table 3 ) ( 9 ): A, subclinical (incidental, asymptomatic) PE; B, symptomatic PE with a low severity score (sPESI 0, PESI ≤85 or Bova ≤4); C, symptomatic PE with an elevated score, subdivided by RV imaging and biomarkers (troponin, natriuretic peptide or lactate) into C1 (both normal), C2 (abnormal RV or biomarker) and C3 (abnormal RV and biomarker); D, incipient cardiopulmonary failure, comprising D1 (transient, fluid-responsive hypotension <15 min) and D2 (normotensive shock, for example lactate >2 mmol/L, oliguria or altered mentation); and E, cardiopulmonary failure, comprising E1 (persistent hypotension with cardiogenic shock) and E2 (refractory shock or cardiac arrest). A respiratory modifier (“R”) is added to categories C–E when hypoxemia, tachypnea or an escalating oxygen requirement is present ( 9 ).

5.3 Side-by-side comparison The correspondence between the frameworks ( Table 3 ) is approximate: categories A and B broadly correspond to ESC low-risk PE; C1 and C2 to intermediate-low risk; and C3, D1 and D2 to intermediate-high risk ( 1 , 9 ). The most important difference lies at the boundary between intermediate- and high-risk disease: patients with transient hypotension (D1) or normotensive shock (D2) represent a more severe stage than C3, but they remain within the ESC intermediate-high-risk class, because the ESC model reserves high risk for cardiac arrest, obstructive shock or persistent hypotension, whereas the AHA/ACC framework recognizes them as a distinct, threatened group in which reperfusion “may be considered” ( 9 ). The AHA/ACC framework also makes lactate measurement (Class 1 in categories C–E), the respiratory modifier and incidental PE explicit, and recommends multidisciplinary PE response team (PERT) evaluation for categories C–E ( 9 ). Conversely, the principles are convergent: hemodynamic status defines urgency, RV dysfunction and myocardial injury refine prognosis in normotensive patients, routine systemic thrombolysis is not recommended in normotensive patients without signs of deterioration, and outpatient care is appropriate for selected low-risk patients ( 1 , 9 ). 5.4 Clinical implications of categories C, D and E Category C comprises hospitalized patients who rarely benefit from therapies beyond anticoagulation; its subdivision by RV imaging and biomarkers, with lactate measurement (Class 1), is intended to identify those at risk of progression ( 9 ). Category C3, particularly with a respiratory modifier, resembles the PEITHO and HI-PEITHO populations, in whom the role of CDI is debated (Section 6.5 ) ( 31 , 32 ).

Category D is the main conceptual advance of the 2026 framework. It recognizes incipient cardiopulmonary failure in patients whose blood pressure is not persistently low: transient, fluid-responsive hypotension (D1) and normotensive shock (D2), defined by markers of hypoperfusion such as lactate >2 mmol/L, acute kidney injury, oliguria, altered mentation or a cardiac index <2.2 L/min/m 2 ( 9 ). In the FLASH registry, approximately one-third of normotensive patients with intermediate-risk PE who underwent invasive hemodynamic assessment had a cardiac index in the shock range ( 33 ), and a composite shock score combining clinical, biochemical and imaging variables has been proposed to identify them non-invasively ( 34 ). Clinically, category D implies admission to an intensive care or high-dependency unit, immediate PERT involvement, avoidance of sedation, intubation and aggressive fluid loading, early vasopressor or inotropic support, and readiness for reperfusion, for which the AHA/ACC guideline assigns a Class 2b recommendation ( 9 ). The evidence base is, however, limited: the concept derives largely from retrospective analyses of patients undergoing mechanical thrombectomy, and no prospective study has yet shown that treating normotensive shock differently improves outcomes ( 9 , 33 ).

Category E corresponds to ESC high-risk PE and mandates immediate reperfusion and circulatory support; by distinguishing refractory shock or arrest (E2), the framework specifies when VA-ECMO is reasonable and surgery without circulatory support is not preferred (Sections 6.3 and 6.6) ( 1 , 9 ).

5.5 Translating categories into monitoring and escalation A single baseline label is insufficient because patients may progress from stable RV strain to incipient failure, a trajectory formalized by the AHA/ACC D categories ( 9 ). In the authors' opinion, the admission note of every patient at ESC intermediate-high risk or in AHA/ACC category C3–D should document explicit escalation triggers (new hypotension, rising lactate, increasing oxygen requirement, syncope, altered mentation, oliguria, progressive tachycardia or worsening RV failure), the pre-agreed rescue strategy and the responsible team, consistent with the recommendation for PERT involvement in these categories ( 1 , 9 ).

6 Acute treatment 6.1 Initial stabilization Supportive therapy should protect RV perfusion and avoid iatrogenic collapse. Because aggressive volume loading may worsen RV dilatation and left ventricular underfilling, cautious fluid administration (≤500 mL) is reserved for patients with low central venous pressure, and norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor for hypotension ( 1 ). Induction of anesthesia and positive-pressure ventilation can precipitate collapse by reducing venous return and increasing RV afterload; the AHA/ACC guideline therefore advises against deep sedation and intubation unless clinically necessary in patients with RV dysfunction ( 1 , 9 ). Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) may stabilize refractory shock or cardiac arrest as a bridge to reperfusion or recovery, but it is not definitive thrombus therapy (Section 6.6 ) ( 9 , 35 ).

6.2 Anticoagulation Anticoagulation should begin promptly, including while awaiting imaging when clinical probability is high or intermediate ( 1 ). Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is preferred over unfractionated heparin (UFH) for parenteral therapy in most patients because of more predictable pharmacokinetics and lower rates of recurrence without increased bleeding ( 1 , 9 ); UFH remains preferable when immediate reperfusion or another procedure is anticipated, when rapid reversal may be needed, and in severe renal impairment ( 1 ). For most eligible adults, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are preferred over vitamin K antagonists (VKAs). In a meta-analysis of the phase 3 trials, DOACs had similar efficacy for recurrent VTE [relative risk (RR) 0.90] and reduced major bleeding (RR 0.61), intracranial hemorrhage (RR 0.37) and fatal bleeding ( 36 – 40 ). Apixaban and rivaroxaban can be started without a parenteral lead-in, whereas dabigatran and edoxaban require at least five days of parenteral anticoagulation. In the randomized COBRRA trial, clinically relevant bleeding during three months of treatment was lower with apixaban than with rivaroxaban (3.3% vs. 7.1%; RR 0.46) ( 41 ).

Drug choice must account for renal and hepatic function, pregnancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, body weight, interactions, adherence, affordability, cancer site, thrombocytopenia and planned procedures ( Table 5 ). In cancer-associated VTE, factor Xa inhibitors were non-inferior or superior to dalteparin for recurrence, but edoxaban and rivaroxaban increased gastrointestinal and genitourinary bleeding in patients with luminal tumors, whereas apixaban did not increase major bleeding (3.8% vs. 4.0%) ( 24 , 42 – 44 ). In high-risk antiphospholipid syndrome, rivaroxaban caused an excess of thrombotic and bleeding events compared with warfarin, and VKAs remain the agents of choice ( 45 ); recommendations for obesity and pregnancy are summarized in Table 5 ( 22 , 46 ).

6.3 Systemic thrombolysis Systemic thrombolysis is recommended for high-risk PE (ESC Class I, level of evidence B; AHA/ACC category E, Class 2a) when bleeding risk is acceptable ( 1 , 9 ). In a meta-analysis of 16 trials, thrombolysis was associated with lower all-cause mortality (odds ratio 0.53) but higher major bleeding (9.24% vs. 3.42%) and intracranial hemorrhage (1.46% vs. 0.19%) ( 47 ). In intermediate-high-risk PE, the PEITHO trial showed that full-dose tenecteplase reduced death or hemodynamic decompensation within 7 days (2.6% vs. 5.6%; odds ratio 0.44), but increased major extracranial bleeding (6.3% vs. 1.2%) and hemorrhagic stroke (2.0% vs. 0.2%), without a mortality advantage ( 32 ). Its long-term follow-up showed no benefit on survival, functional limitation or CTEPH (Section 9.2 ) ( 48 ). Accordingly, both guidelines recommend against routine systemic thrombolysis in normotensive patients (ESC Class III; AHA/ACC categories A–C2, Class 3: Harm) and favor anticoagulation with close monitoring and rescue reperfusion if deterioration occurs (ESC Class I for rescue thrombolysis) ( 1 , 9 ). For categories D1–D2, systemic thrombolysis “may be considered” (Class 2b) ( 9 ).

Reduced-dose thrombolysis is attractive: 50 mg of alteplase was as effective as 100 mg on radiological endpoints with fewer bleeding events ( 49 ), but such trials have been underpowered for clinical outcomes. The ongoing PEITHO-3 trial is randomizing approximately 650 patients with intermediate-high-risk PE and additional clinical markers of severity to reduced-dose alteplase or placebo on top of heparin, with a 30-day composite of death, hemodynamic decompensation or recurrent PE as the primary outcome ( 50 ). Contraindications should be weighed against the threat of imminent death from obstructive shock ( 1 ).

6.4 Catheter-directed intervention: terminology and evidence For clarity, we use catheter-directed intervention (CDI) as an umbrella term for percutaneous reperfusion techniques, comprising two families ( 11 , 12 ). Local (catheter-directed) thrombolysis delivers a low total dose of fibrinolytic—typically 8–24 mg of alteplase over several hours—through standard multi-side-hole catheters (conventional catheter-directed thrombolysis, CDT) or ultrasound-facilitated catheters (USCDT). Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) removes thrombus without, or with minimal, fibrinolytic exposure, using large-bore aspiration or extraction systems or computer-assisted vacuum thrombectomy. Early evidence consisted of single-arm studies or small randomized trials with surrogate endpoints, chiefly the reduction in the RV-to-left ventricular (RV/LV) diameter ratio at 24–48 h: ULTIMA, SEATTLE II, OPTALYSE and SUNSET sPE for local thrombolysis ( 51 – 54 ), and FLARE, EXTRACT-PE and the 800-patient FLASH registry for MT ( 55 – 57 ). In high-risk PE, the non-randomized FLAME study reported in-hospital mortality of 1.9% with large-bore MT versus 29.5% in a context arm treated predominantly with systemic thrombolysis, although the groups were not comparable, so these data represent observational evidence only ( 58 ). The small CANARY trial was stopped early without a significant difference in its primary endpoint ( 59 ) ( Table 7 ).

The evidence base has changed substantially with four randomized trials ( Table 7 ). HI-PEITHO randomized 544 patients with intermediate-high-risk PE (RV/LV ≥1.0, elevated troponin) and at least two markers of physiological stress (heart rate ≥100/min, SBP ≤110 mmHg, respiratory rate ≥20/min or oxygen saturation ≤90%) to USCDT plus anticoagulation or anticoagulation alone ( 31 ). The 7-day composite of PE-related death, cardiorespiratory decompensation or collapse, or symptomatic recurrence occurred in 4.0% versus 10.3% (RR 0.39; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.20–0.77), corresponding to a number needed to treat of approximately 16. The effect was driven by cardiorespiratory decompensation (3.7% vs. 10.3%), defined to include a National Early Warning Score ≥9; PE-related death (1.1% vs. 0.4%) and 30-day all-cause mortality (1.8% vs. 1.1%) did not differ, there was no intracranial hemorrhage, and 7-day major bleeding was numerically but not significantly higher (4.1% vs. 2.2%) ( 31 ). In PEERLESS (550 patients), large-bore MT was superior to CDT on a hierarchical win ratio (5.01; 95% CI 3.68–6.97) driven by less clinical deterioration or bailout (1.8% vs. 5.4%) and lower intensive care unit (ICU) use, without differences in mortality or bleeding ( 60 ). In STORM-PE (100 patients), computer-assisted vacuum thrombectomy plus anticoagulation reduced the 48-hour RV/LV ratio more than anticoagulation alone (0.52 vs. 0.24) ( 61 ).

HI-PEITHO is thus the first adequately powered randomized trial to show that a CDI reduces early clinical deterioration. However, it was open-label and industry-funded, enrolled highly selected patients at experienced centers, relied on a composite in which a physiological score contributed substantially, and did not show reductions in mortality; long-term functional outcomes are pending ( 31 ). PEERLESS compared two interventional strategies with a resource-driven endpoint, and STORM-PE used a surrogate endpoint ( 60 , 61 ). Ongoing trials, including PEERLESS II (large-bore MT versus anticoagulation), PE-TRACT (CDI versus anticoagulation with functional endpoints) and PEITHO-3, will further define net benefit (Section 11 ).

6.5 Elective CDI in intermediate-high-risk PE with several adverse prognostic markers Whether such patients should undergo elective CDI rather than anticoagulation with rescue therapy is the most debated question in acute PE care. Arguments in favor include the 61% relative reduction in early decompensation in HI-PEITHO ( 31 ), the low rates of intracranial hemorrhage with CDI compared with systemic thrombolysis ( 31 , 47 , 60 ), and the position statement of the Spanish Society of Cardiology, which suggests considering elective CDI within 24 h in intermediate-high-risk patients with multiple poor prognostic factors (for example, elevated lactate, syncope, borderline blood pressure or tachycardia) ( 12 ). The AHA/ACC guideline assigns a Class 2b recommendation (benefit unclear) to CDI in categories C2–C3 and “may be considered” in D1–D2 ( 9 ). Arguments for caution include the absence of a mortality benefit, the lack of long-term benefit after thrombolysis in PEITHO ( 48 ), procedural complications ( 12 , 62 ), costs, unequal access, and the fact that most patients treated with anticoagulation alone in HI-PEITHO and PEITHO did not deteriorate ( 31 , 32 ).

CDI-related complications can be grouped into access-site and vascular complications (hematoma, inadvertent arterial puncture, retroperitoneal hemorrhage, pseudoaneurysm and arteriovenous fistula); bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage when a fibrinolytic is used; injury to the pulmonary arteries (perforation or pseudoaneurysm, presenting with hemoptysis, hemothorax or desaturation) or to the right heart (tricuspid valve damage, perforation or tamponade, and arrhythmias including atrioventricular block); periprocedural hemodynamic deterioration; and device-related problems such as catheter entrapment or kinking ( 62 ). Their reported frequency varies widely, because definitions are not standardized and reporting windows range from 48 h to 90 days ( 62 ). In the randomized trials and prospective registries summarized in a recent expert review, access-site complications occurred in approximately 1%–8% of patients, the overall rate of pulmonary artery injury was around 0.7%, and intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 0%–2% ( 62 ). Major bleeding ranged from approximately 1% with large-bore MT in the FLASH registry to approximately 7% with either MT or CDT in PEERLESS and 10% with USCDT in SEATTLE II, and it reached 11% after MT in high-risk patients in FLAME ( 54 , 55 , 58 , 60 ). Randomized trials report no or very low procedural mortality, whereas real-world data report CDI-related mortality of 3.5%–6.7%, and in the US Food and Drug Administration Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) database, pulmonary vascular perforation was the most common complication resulting in death after mechanical thrombectomy ( 62 ). Large-bore aspiration also entails blood loss, which is now mitigated by blood-return systems ( 12 ). These data support performing CDI at experienced centers, with real-time ultrasound-guided venous access, careful catheter and guidewire manipulation and predefined bail-out options such as systemic thrombolysis or surgery, and weighing the expected benefit against procedural risk in each patient ( 12 , 62 ).

Thus, the evidence supporting elective CDI consists of one randomized trial with an early clinical endpoint, surrogate-endpoint trials and registries, and expert consensus. In the authors' opinion, pending PEITHO-3, PEERLESS II and PE-TRACT, elective CDI is reasonable after PERT discussion for patients who meet HI-PEITHO-like criteria (ESC intermediate-high risk or AHA/ACC category C3 with at least two markers of physiological stress) or AHA/ACC category D1–D2, have low procedural risk and are treated at experienced centers; other normotensive patients should receive anticoagulation with monitoring and a predefined rescue strategy.

6.6 High-risk PE when systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed For high-risk PE with a contraindication to, or failure of, systemic thrombolysis, the ESC recommends surgical embolectomy (Class I, level C) and suggests percutaneous catheter-directed treatment as an alternative (Class IIa, level C) ( 1 ); the AHA/ACC guideline considers local thrombolysis, MT and surgical embolectomy reasonable in category E1 (Class 2a) and VA-ECMO reasonable in category E2 with refractory shock (Class 2a) ( 9 ). No randomized trial has compared MT with local thrombolysis in this setting, so their relative roles rest on mechanistic reasoning, registry data and expert consensus rather than on comparative trials ( 11 , 12 , 58 ). MT provides immediate debulking without fibrinolytic exposure and is generally preferred when the contraindication is absolute (for example, recent intracranial hemorrhage or active bleeding) or when the patient cannot await a multi-hour infusion; local thrombolysis, which still exposes the patient to a low-dose fibrinolytic, may be considered when contraindications are relative, when MT is unavailable, or after incomplete mechanical debulking ( 11 , 12 ). In refractory shock or cardiac arrest, VA-ECMO can serve as a bridge to MT or surgical embolectomy; observational case series suggest better outcomes when ECMO is combined with definitive reperfusion than when it is used as stand-alone therapy, but no randomized data exist ( 9 , 35 ).

6.7 Surgical embolectomy, right-heart thrombus and PE response teams Surgical embolectomy is an option for high-risk PE when thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed, and for thrombus in transit or straddling a patent foramen ovale ( 1 , 9 ); outcomes depend heavily on selection and experience, with an in-hospital mortality of 27.2% in a nationwide United States cohort ( 63 ). Evidence for surgical embolectomy is limited to observational series. Management of right-heart thrombus should be individualized by a multidisciplinary team according to hemodynamic status, thrombus mobility and size, bleeding risk, patent foramen ovale and local expertise, as randomized evidence is lacking ( 1 ). The AHA/ACC guideline recommends multidisciplinary PERT evaluation for categories C–E (Class 1) ( 9 ). This recommendation rests on observational before-and-after studies: in a meta-analysis, PERT implementation increased the use of advanced therapies (RR 2.67), whereas the reduction in mortality was not significant (RR 0.89; 95% CI 0.67–1.19) ( 64 , 65 ). A PERT should therefore be judged by timeliness, appropriateness, complications and patient-centered outcomes, not by procedural volume (authors' opinion).

6.8 Inferior vena cava filters Inferior vena cava filters do not treat PE. In PREPIC2, adding a retrievable filter to anticoagulation did not reduce recurrent PE at three months (3.0% vs. 1.5%; RR 2.00) ( 66 ). Filters should be reserved for acute VTE with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation or recurrence despite adequate anticoagulation, with a documented retrieval plan ( 1 , 9 ).

7 Transitions of care: disposition, discharge and early follow-up 7.1 Outpatient treatment and early discharge Selected low-risk patients (ESC low risk; AHA/ACC categories A–B) can be treated at home or discharged early ( 1 , 9 ). Outpatient treatment was non-inferior to inpatient care in the randomized OTPE trial (recurrent VTE 0.6% vs. 0% at 90 days) ( 67 ); early discharge on rivaroxaban was associated with recurrent VTE or PE-related death in 0.6% in HoT-PE ( 68 ); and in HOME-PE, Hestia- and sPESI-based triage yielded similar 30-day adverse outcomes (3.8% vs. 3.6%) ( 69 ). A low clinical score is necessary but not sufficient. Oxygen requirement, bleeding risk, renal function, comorbidity, pain control, medication access, health literacy and social support must also be favorable ( 30 , 69 ). In the authors' opinion, when medication access, housing, transport, language support or follow-up are unreliable, a brief admission may be safer than nominally guideline-concordant discharge.

7.2 The minimum discharge bundle In the authors' experience, the most preventable anticoagulant errors occur at transitions: the initial high-dose phase of apixaban and rivaroxaban, the parenteral lead-in for dabigatran and edoxaban, VKA overlap, duplication with residual heparin and prescriptions that do not cover the initiation phase. We therefore propose a minimum discharge bundle ( Table 8 ) that specifies the drug, dose and date of any dose change, the provisional duration and provoking context, bleeding mitigation, warning signs and a named clinician responsible for follow-up. The bundle operationalizes the AHA/ACC recommendations for clinical contact within the first week after discharge (Class 1), a visit at or before three months to decide on anticoagulation duration (Class 1), and systematic enquiry about PE-related symptoms and functional limitation at every visit for at least one year (Class 1) ( 9 ), as well as the ESC recommendation for routine re-evaluation three to six months after acute PE (Class I) ( 1 , 4 ).

7.3 Communication and shared decision-making Shared decision-making is essential when evidence supports more than one reasonable strategy: surveillance versus anticoagulation for isolated subsegmental PE, finite versus extended therapy, reduced-dose secondary prevention, elective CDI, and intervention for symptomatic CTEPD without resting pulmonary hypertension ( 4 , 9 ). The AHA/ACC guideline considers screening for anxiety and depression reasonable (Class 2a) ( 9 ). In the authors' opinion, explaining hemodynamic risk and the expected recovery trajectory is more informative for patients than anatomical terms such as “massive”.

8 Duration of anticoagulation and secondary prevention 8.1 The duration decision All patients require at least three months of therapeutic anticoagulation; thereafter, the decision balances the risk of recurrence if treatment stops, the risk of bleeding if it continues, and patient preference ( 1 , 9 ). After a first unprovoked VTE, the cumulative risk of recurrence after stopping anticoagulation is approximately 10% at one year, 16% at two years, 25% at five years and 36% at ten years ( 15 ). A major transient provoking factor, such as major surgery, supports discontinuation after three months, whereas unprovoked PE, persistent risk factors, active cancer and recurrent VTE favor extended therapy ( 1 , 14 , 26 , 71 ). The AHA/ACC guideline recommends continuing anticoagulation—with reduced-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban as an option—after the initial three months unless the PE was a first event strongly provoked by a transient risk factor (Class 1) ( 9 ).

Reduced-dose DOACs combine efficacy with a favorable bleeding profile. In AMPLIFY-EXT, recurrent VTE or VTE-related death occurred in 8.8% with placebo versus 1.7% with apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, with similar major bleeding ( 72 ); in EINSTEIN CHOICE, recurrence was 1.2% with rivaroxaban 10 mg versus 4.4% with aspirin ( 73 ). In RENOVE, which enrolled patients at high risk of recurrence, reduced-dose DOACs were non-inferior to full-dose DOACs for recurrent VTE (2.2% vs. 1.8%) and reduced clinically relevant bleeding (9.9% vs. 15.2%; hazard ratio 0.61) ( 74 ). In API-CAT, reduced-dose apixaban was non-inferior to full-dose apixaban for extended treatment of cancer-associated VTE (recurrence 2.1% vs. 2.8%), with less clinically relevant bleeding (12.1% vs. 15.6%) ( 75 ).

8.2 Dynamic reassessment of bleeding risk Bleeding risk is dynamic: age, kidney function, anemia, antiplatelet or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, uncontrolled hypertension, alcohol, falls and prior bleeding should be reviewed at each visit and modified where possible ( 1 , 4 ). In the authors' opinion, neither a previous PE nor a bleeding score should replace shared decision-making, and in older adults falls rarely justify withholding anticoagulation in isolation.

8.3 Special populations In cancer-associated PE, thrombotic and bleeding risks vary with tumor site, mucosal involvement, anticancer therapy, thrombocytopenia and prognosis, and anticoagulation generally continues while cancer is active ( 24 ). Thrombocytopenia requires a graded strategy; full-dose anticoagulation is usually continued above 50 × 10⁹/L, whereas dose reduction, platelet support or temporary interruption are considered below this threshold depending on clot burden and time from the acute event ( 76 ). After estrogen-associated PE, estrogen-containing contraception is usually replaced by progestin-only or nonhormonal methods before anticoagulation ends; in an analysis of the EINSTEIN trials, continuing hormonal therapy during anticoagulation was not associated with an excess of recurrent VTE, whereas abnormal uterine bleeding was more frequent with rivaroxaban than with enoxaparin/VKA ( 77 ). Pregnancy-associated PE is treated with LMWH for at least six weeks postpartum and for a minimum total duration of three months, and future pregnancies require a prophylaxis plan ( 1 , 22 ). In severe or rapidly changing renal dysfunction, UFH may offer controllability, and DOAC selection must reflect drug clearance ( 1 ).

8.4 Suspected recurrence during anticoagulation Suspected recurrence requires objective confirmation and comparison with previous imaging, because residual abnormalities may persist ( 1 , 4 ). The evaluation should establish the drug and dose, adherence, interruptions, malabsorption, renal and hepatic function and interacting medication; when recurrence is confirmed despite verified exposure, cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia should be considered, and a temporary switch to LMWH is commonly used (authors' opinion).

9 Post-PE syndrome, CTEPD and CTEPH 9.1 Definitions and hemodynamic thresholds The post-pulmonary embolism (post-PE) syndrome is an umbrella term for new or persistent dyspnea, exercise limitation or impaired quality of life after at least three months of adequate anticoagulation that is not explained by other conditions ( 4 , 5 ). It comprises distinct phenotypes ( Table 9 ): symptoms without demonstrable cardiopulmonary impairment, frequently related to deconditioning or dysfunctional breathing; post-PE cardiac impairment with persistent RV dysfunction; CTEPD without pulmonary hypertension; and CTEPH ( 4 ). According to the 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines, pulmonary hypertension is defined at right-heart catheterization by a mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) > 20 mmHg, and pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension additionally requires a pulmonary arterial wedge pressure (PAWP) ≤ 15 mmHg and a PVR >2 Wood units (WU); exercise pulmonary hypertension is defined by an mPAP/cardiac output slope >3 mmHg/L/min between rest and exercise ( 10 ). CTEPH is pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension with mismatched perfusion defects and imaging signs of chronic thromboembolic obstruction after at least three months of effective anticoagulation ( 8 , 10 ). CTEPD is the broader term for symptomatic patients with these perfusion defects and chronic thromboembolic changes, with or without pulmonary hypertension at rest ( 8 , 10 ).

9.2 Frequency and the effect of acute reperfusion Persistent limitation is common. In the prospective ELOPE cohort, 46.6% of patients had a peak oxygen uptake below 80% of predicted one year after PE ( 6 ). In FOCUS, the two-year cumulative incidence of post-PE impairment was 16.0% and that of CTEPH 2.3%; post-PE impairment identified 15 of the 16 patients eventually diagnosed with CTEPH ( 7 ). A meta-analysis estimated the incidence of CTEPH at 0.56% in all-comers, 3.2% in survivors and 2.8% in survivors without major comorbidities ( 78 ), consistent with earlier prospective cohorts reporting 1.5% and 3.8% at two years ( 79 , 80 ). Reperfusion has not been shown to prevent chronic sequelae: in the three-year follow-up of PEITHO, tenecteplase did not reduce CTEPH (2.1% vs. 3.2%), persistent dyspnea or functional limitation (36.0% vs. 30.1%), or residual pulmonary hypertension and RV dysfunction on echocardiography ( 48 ). Whether CDI modifies long-term outcomes is unknown, and the long-term data of HI-PEITHO and PE-TRACT are awaited ( 31 ).

9.3 Structured follow-up and screening algorithms A visit at approximately three months is the clinical anchor of follow-up ( 1 , 4 , 9 ). The Post-VTE Functional Status (PVFS) scale and the disease-specific Pulmonary Embolism Quality of Life (PEmb-QoL) questionnaire allow standardized and serial assessment ( 81 , 82 ). Routine imaging of asymptomatic patients and screening for CTEPH in asymptomatic survivors are not recommended (ESC Class III) ( 1 ), whereas symptomatic patients with mismatched perfusion defects beyond three months should be referred to a pulmonary hypertension/CTEPH center (ESC Class I) ( 1 ).

The ESC position paper proposes echocardiography for patients with persistent dyspnea, functional limitation or CTEPH risk factors, followed by V/Q scintigraphy and referral when pulmonary hypertension is probable ( 4 ). In the InShape II management study (424 patients), an algorithm combining the CTEPH prediction score with electrocardiography and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) excluded CTEPH without echocardiography in 81% of patients, with a failure rate of 0.29% during two years, and identified 10 of the 13 CTEPH cases within four months ( 83 ). In InShape IV, adding a dedicated reading of the index CTPA for signs of chronic thromboembolism reduced the failure rate to 0%, with 20%–24% of patients requiring echocardiography ( 84 ), underlining the value of handing forward acute-phase imaging findings. A recent Delphi study among 39 European experts reached consensus that the three-month visit should assess the full spectrum of sequelae (CTEPH, CTEPD and post-PE syndrome) using patient-reported outcomes, that CPET is useful in persistent dyspnea, that right-heart catheterization belongs in specialized centers, that patients with persistent dyspnea need extended follow-up even after CTEPH and CTEPD are excluded, and that a single uniform protocol is preferable ( 85 , 86 ). Our pathway integrating these elements is shown in Figure 2 ; its screening components rest on prospective management studies, whereas visit timing and multidisciplinary organization rest on expert consensus ( 4 , 85 ).
